\subsection{Data Collection and Political-Corruption Classifier}
\label{sec:method-political-classifier}

% Generated by political_classifier/scripts/07_build_attention_outputs.py.
\input{tables/attention/latex/political_corruption_manuscript_values}

News articles were collected as part of the RESPOND multilingual news corpus. The data-collection workflow queried the News API using country-specific corruption keyword dictionaries with declensions and morphological variants. The collection code and keyword-generation notebooks are maintained in the related RESPOND media repository.\footnote{\url{https://github.com/annekroon/RESPOND_media/tree/main/data-collection/news-collection/news-api}} The present repository starts from the \PCRawQueryN{} exported country-level query results and implements the cleaning, deduplication, source screening, classification, and validation workflow used to identify articles primarily about political corruption.

The first stage cleaned and deduplicated each country-level news file independently. Article text was standardized by using the combined title/body field available in the exported data and storing it as \texttt{article\_text}. Text normalization removed excess whitespace and repaired common character-encoding artefacts. Rows marked as duplicates by the source data were removed, articles with missing text or fewer than 80 words were excluded, and duplicate URIs and exact duplicate normalized texts were removed within country using SHA-256 hashes. Prefix-based near-duplicate removal was not used in the production run because common article leads can occur in substantively different stories. The resulting cleaned corpus contained \PCCleanedQueryN{} articles from Bulgaria, France, Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, Serbia, Sweden, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom.

The cleaned corpus was subsequently restricted to conventional journalistic outlets. Each country--source pair was evaluated on whether the outlet was genuinely based in the assigned country, produced original reporting or exercised identifiable editorial curation, and did not function primarily as an official repository, press-release distributor, or automated aggregator. The reviewed source workbook records the final decision in \texttt{conventional\_journalism}. Only sources explicitly coded \texttt{Yes} were retained; sources coded \texttt{No}, left unresolved, or missing from the workbook were excluded. This screen reduced the cleaned corruption-query corpus to \PCSourceFilteredN{} articles. Source eligibility was applied before constructing the silver-labelled training sample and before scoring the final corpus.

The second stage trained a classifier to distinguish articles primarily about political corruption from articles that mention corruption only incidentally or concern non-political misconduct. Political corruption was defined as the misuse of public or political office, authority, or resources for private or political gain. The positive class includes articles focused on allegations, investigations, charges, or proven instances of corruption by political officials. Articles focused on private fraud, ordinary crime, or misconduct by non-political actors were treated as negative cases.

Because manual labels were limited, we used a silver-labeling strategy. A country-balanced candidate set was sampled from the source-filtered corpus and sent to the UvA LLM proxy for structured political-corruption labels. These labels were treated as silver labels for model training rather than as final human annotations. A manually annotated validation set was kept separate for evaluation. After an initial country-level validation check showed low positive support for the United Kingdom, 50 additional UK cases were manually reviewed and added as a validation-only supplement. The benchmark was restricted to the same source-eligible population as the production corpus. URI and normalized-text overlap between the silver set and this benchmark was removed before training and checked with a hard zero-overlap assertion.

Candidate classifiers were evaluated against the human benchmark. Before fitting, the eligible benchmark was divided once, with a fixed seed and stratification by country and class, into a threshold-calibration partition (\PCCalibrationN{} articles) and a held-out reporting partition (\PCHeldOutN{} articles). The final selected classifier used \texttt{intfloat/}\allowbreak\texttt{multilingual-e5-large} sentence embeddings and a class-balanced logistic regression model trained on \PCSilverTrainN{} source-filtered silver-labelled articles. The threshold was selected only on the calibration partition and fixed at \PCThreshold{}. On the held-out partition, the classifier achieved accuracy = \PCTestAccuracy{}, political-corruption precision = \PCTestPrecision{}, political-corruption recall = \PCTestRecall{}, political-corruption F1 = \PCTestFOne{}, macro F1 = \PCTestMacroFOne{}, and weighted F1 = \PCTestWeightedFOne{}. Human-label five-fold cross-validation models are reported only as diagnostics. The main classifier validation results are reported in Table~\ref{tab:pc-classifier-comparison-main}; the calibration threshold sweep and held-out country results are provided in Appendix Tables~\ref{tab:pc-classifier-threshold-sweep} and~\ref{tab:pc-classifier-country-validation}.

The final classifier was applied to the \PCSourceFilteredN{} source-filtered country records. Articles with predicted probabilities at or above \PCThreshold{} were retained, producing a final political-corruption corpus of \PCFinalN{} articles, or \PCFinalShare\% of the source-filtered corruption-query corpus. These articles form the input for subsequent analyses of victim visibility, corruption framing, case location, accused-actor visibility, and attention over time. For descriptive attention analyses, the numerator is the number of final political-corruption articles in a country-period. The denominator comes from a separate NewsAPI country-period total-news count series rather than from the corruption-query corpus. Because the available total-news counts are not source-specific, this denominator represents the broader collected news universe and is not filtered using the outlet-inclusion workbook. Figure~\ref{fig:pc-data-pipeline} summarizes these two collection routes and their analytical uses; country-specific construction counts are reported in Table~\ref{tab:pc-corpus-construction-country-summary}.
